highlights: The largest medieval fortress on the Middle Rhine, built in 1245, considered impregnable for 450 years until French forces razed it in 1794
One of the largest and best-preserved fortress ruins in the Rhine Gorge, opposite the Loreley rock
The hotel's 67 rooms are split across three separate structures: the historic castle building, an Art Nouveau villa (Villa Rheinfels), and an apartment house on the Gut Rheinfels grounds

description:
Rheinfels Castle, built in 1245, was the largest medieval fortress on the Middle Rhine and earned a reputation for near-invincibility that lasted roughly 450 years — surviving sieges that destroyed lesser Rhine strongholds. That long defensive record ended in 1794, when French revolutionary forces swept through the region and razed the fortress, leaving behind the extensive ruins that still dominate the hillside above St. Goar today, directly across the river from the famous Loreley rock.

Rather than being rebuilt as a single reconstructed building, Rheinfels today operates as a hotel spread across three distinct structures on the historic grounds: the ruined castle itself, an Art Nouveau villa (Villa Rheinfels) built later on the estate, and a separate apartment house at Gut Rheinfels. The 67 rooms across these three buildings give guests free access to explore one of the most substantial fortress ruins on the entire Rhine, a genuinely different experience from castle-hotels where the historic structure has been fully rebuilt into a conventional hotel building.

The scale of Rheinfels' surviving ruins sets it apart even among the Rhine Gorge's many castle sites: extensive underground passages, gun batteries and fortification walls remain explorable, giving visitors a far more immersive sense of a genuine medieval-to-early-modern fortress than the smaller ruins or fully rebuilt castles found elsewhere along the river. For day visitors not staying overnight, the ruins are separately ticketed, making Rheinfels one of the more substantial standalone visitor attractions among the castle-hotels covered in this collection.

The castle's position directly opposite the Loreley rock places it at one of the most photographed and mythologised points on the entire Rhine. The Loreley legend — a siren whose song lured sailors to their deaths on the rocks below — has drawn visitors and artists to this stretch of the gorge for centuries, and Rheinfels' hillside position gives hotel guests a direct, elevated view across the river to the rock itself.

The Upper Middle Rhine Valley's UNESCO World Heritage designation recognises exactly this combination found at Rheinfels: dramatic fortress ruins, terraced vineyards and a river landscape that together tell the story of centuries of trade, conflict and settlement along one of Europe's most strategically important waterways. Rheinfels' scale and survival as ruins, rather than a fully reconstructed building, make it one of the more historically legible sites within that wider UNESCO landscape.

St. Goar itself, the small Rhine town beneath the castle, retains much of its historic character and gives guests a walkable base for exploring both the ruins above and the riverfront below, including boat excursions that pass directly beneath the Loreley rock on the opposite bank.

The division of Rheinfels' guest accommodation across three separate historic and later buildings reflects the practical reality of operating a hotel within a genuine ruin: rather than compromising the fortress's authenticity with extensive new construction inside the ruins themselves, the hotel expanded into the Art Nouveau villa and the Gut Rheinfels apartment house nearby, preserving the ruins largely as they have stood since their 1794 destruction while still offering modern hotel accommodation on the same historic estate.

Among the surviving structures, visitors can explore extensive underground passages and gun batteries cut into the hillside, remnants of the fortress's defensive engineering that go well beyond the wall fragments and foundations typical of many smaller Rhine ruins. These passages give a genuinely tangible sense of the scale and sophistication of Rheinfels' original fortifications, built to withstand exactly the kind of prolonged siege warfare that eventually proved impossible to resist against Napoleonic-era artillery.

St. Goar's own riverfront, a short walk downhill from the ruins, offers boat excursions along this stretch of the Rhine Gorge, giving guests a complementary river-level perspective on the same landscape they survey from the fortress heights above — a useful pairing for visitors wanting both the historical and scenic dimensions of a Rhine Gorge stay in a single visit.
history: Rheinfels Castle was built in 1245 and became the largest medieval fortress on the Middle Rhine, considered impregnable for roughly 450 years until French revolutionary forces razed it in 1794. The extensive ruins that resulted still dominate the hillside above St. Goar, directly across the Rhine from the Loreley rock. Today the site operates as a hotel spread across three structures — the ruined castle, the Art Nouveau Villa Rheinfels, and an apartment house at Gut Rheinfels — with free ruins access for overnight guests, within the UNESCO-listed Upper Middle Rhine Valley.

faqs.question: Can I visit the Rheinfels Castle ruins without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes — the extensive fortress ruins, among the largest on the Middle Rhine, are separately ticketed for day visitors. Overnight hotel guests receive free access as part of their stay.

faqs.question: Are all the hotel rooms inside the castle ruins?
faqs.answer: No. The 67 rooms are split across three separate buildings on the historic grounds: part of the ruined castle itself, the Art Nouveau Villa Rheinfels, and an apartment house at Gut Rheinfels.

faqs.question: Why was Rheinfels Castle destroyed?
faqs.answer: After roughly 450 years as the largest and most formidable fortress on the Middle Rhine, considered impregnable, it was razed by French revolutionary forces in 1794, leaving the extensive ruins that survive today.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** St. Goar, Rhineland-Palatinate, on the Rhine Gorge opposite the Loreley rock.

**Rooms & rates:** The 67 rooms are split across three separate buildings on the historic grounds: part of the ruined castle itself, the Art Nouveau Villa Rheinfels, and an apartment house at Gut Rheinfels. From €108/night.

**On-site:** Restaurant, gardens, free guest access to the fortress ruins.

**Good to know:** This is one of the more architecturally complex properties in the collection — ask specifically which of the three buildings a room is in if sleeping within the actual medieval ruins (rather than the villa or apartment house) is the priority.

**Combine with:** The Loreley rock and visitor centre, directly across the river.
